In February 1862, less than a year into the Civil War, Willie died of what was likely typhoid fever. President Lincoln was reportedly inconsolable. According to an account that has passed into legend, he returned to the crypt at Georgetown’s Oak Hill Cemetery, opened his son’s coffin, and held his body in his arms. Whether this extraordinary act of mourning actually occurred remains uncertain; its dramatic possibilities, however, prove irresistible. Here was the man charged with preserving a nation yet incapable of preserving the life of his child.

Lincoln in the Bardo derives a great deal of emotional force from this contradiction, but the novel is also about the difficulty of historical knowledge. Saunders’s competing accounts of a White House reception, held while Willie lay gravely ill upstairs, expose the fragility of the historical record. Throughout the novel, witnesses disagree about the atmosphere of his gathering, the weather, and the president’s appearance. Their testimony accumulates without producing certainty. History, Saunders implies, is not a coherent account of what happened but a collection of incompatible recollections, compiled afterward into something resembling meaning. Much of the historical material that gives the novel its peculiar authority, however, has been stripped from the opera. It is the invented inhabitants of the cemetery, rather than the historical figures who wander through it, who give the story its uncanny power.

The opera’s more static characters provided some of its liveliest musical episodes. Stephanie Blythe and Craig Colclough as the crass, tosspot Barons inhabited a world of abrasive domestic comedy, their exchanges exposing the persistence of petty grievances beyond the grave. In their scenes the music’s rhythmic irregularities, interruptions, and emphatic accents delivered a useful counterweight to the score’s prevailing lyric melancholy. The other ghosts offered a different kind of musical characterization. Ryan McKinny’s Vollman and Jonah Hoskins’s Bevins formed an unlikely comic partnership, their contrasting vocal registers and temperaments suggesting two incompatible forms of attachment. McKinny’s earthy bass-baritone gave Vollman’s extravagant bodily predicament a bizarre solidity, while Hoskins’s brighter tenor seemed continually drawn upward toward the sensations and possibilities that Bevins had abandoned in life. Their exchanges frequently approached patter, with words tumbling over one another in a manner that recalled the ensembles of earlier comic operas.

The opera’s grotesquerie assumes a more troubling dimension when the absurdity of the bardo gives way to the terror of what lies beyond it. The Reverend knows more about death than the others, but he fears the damnation to which he has seen he will be condemned in the afterlife. His music therefore combines something like prophetic grandeur with the desperation of a man attempting to postpone judgment. The casting of a dramatic soprano, Christine Goerke, as a male clergyman introduced an ambiguity that suited the bardo’s disregard for ordinary categories. Her foghorn-like voice (that’s a compliment) can move from comic exaggeration to a more unsettling tone, and the Reverend’s Act Two revelation of the fate he has tried to avoid gives Mazzoli an opportunity for some of her most exuberant vocal writing.

Anthony Roth Costanzo, in drag as Miss Elise Traynor, who died at fourteen, represents another kind of suspension. Elise’s expectations of motherhood have been permanently arrested, and she has become a garish embodiment of futures that will never arrive. Costanzo’s countertenor, with its strangely disembodied brilliance, expressed her despair, although his performance sometimes seemed more indebted to the theatrical possibilities of eccentricity than to the quieter horror of Elise’s predicament.

Lincoln occupies a peculiarly unstable position here. His anguish over Willie is genuine, but it exists alongside a catastrophe in which countless other families are experiencing comparable losses. The president’s private sorrow is therefore both singular and representative. He cannot mourn his son without confronting the larger machinery of death over which he presides. Saunders makes this tension especially apparent through formerly enslaved characters who expose the limits of the novel’s more sentimental understanding of suffering. Death may eventually unite everyone, but it does not erase inequalities. The cemetery is not a democratic republic simply because all its inhabitants are dead.

Thomas Havens and Mrs. Francis Hodge, sung affectively by Joshua Blue and Janai Brugger, bring this dimension into the opera. Havens’s enslavement cannot be reduced to another variation on personal attachment, because his life was shaped by a political and economic system whose consequences extend far beyond individual psychology. Here the opera’s historical setting becomes more than a picturesque backdrop. Lincoln’s grief is not merely the suffering of a father. It is the suffering of a man whose decisions will help determine the fate of millions and whose understanding of that responsibility is inseparable from his experience of mortality. Mazzoli’s score isn’t as explicit about these political implications as Saunders’s novel. Emotionally the opera remains focused primarily on Lincoln’s acceptance of his son’s death. This narrowing shifts the work’s moral balance.

Lileana Blain-Cruz’s production, designed by Adam Rigg, approached the cemetery as a landscape of distorted consciousness. Its rank vegetation, strange colors, and immense proportions suggested a natural environment that had continued to grow despite its inhabitants having lost the ability to change. The stage became an overgrown repository of unfinished lives. James Ortiz’s enormous puppets, meanwhile, gave external form to psychological conditions. Their outsize shapes and disconcerting movements implied that the dead had become inseparable from their own obsessions. This was an intelligent solution to the novel’s peculiar physical vocabulary. Saunders’s ghosts are not ethereal beings floating through a divine afterlife. They are paradoxically material, their bodies transformed by the very desires that prevent their departure. Blain-Cruz recognized that the supernatural need not be weightless. Her bardo was crowded, tactile, sometimes repellent.

The production’s visual imagination was at once its greatest strength and its most persistent frustration. As in so many new Met productions, the stage was littered with the unnecessary additions of supernumeraries and dancers. The choreographer, Raja Feather Kelly, often had them engaged in ceaseless, vaguely symbolic activity, as though the emotional significance of a scene could be measured by the number of bodies occupying it. They assembled, writhed, and dispersed, supplying a visual commentary that rather than enriching the music suggested a distrust of its capacity to speak for itself. One began to suspect that stillness, in the contemporary operatic imagination, has become something to be avoided at all costs, even when the music is asking us to listen.

The problem was not necessarily the spectacle; it was that the spectacle could make mystery too comprehensible. Saunders’s novel is unsettling partly because the reader must imagine a universe whose rules are never entirely explained. Blain-Cruz’s production, by contrast, sometimes offered an illustration for every uncertainty. There were swinging branches, elaborate apparitions, projections, pyrotechnics, even a live horse. At moments the stage appeared to be a kind of metaphysical theme park, as though the audience had to be continually reminded that it had entered an extraordinary realm. When a soul departed in an explosion of light, the effect was theatrically satisfying but conceptually literal. The terrifying “matterlightblooming phenomenon” that the novel presents as almost beyond the capacity of language became another part in the stage machinery.

There is something distinctly American about the opera’s preoccupation with unfinished lives. The bardo’s cemetery is populated by people who remain convinced that they have not yet exhausted their opportunities. They expect another chance, another conversation, another morning in which the ordinary business of existence can resume—a distorted extension of the national faith in perpetual possibility.

Mazzoli has attempted to create a musical drama in which the usual distinctions between comedy and tragedy, life and death, historical reality and supernatural invention are continually destabilized. An intriguing question posed by Lincoln in the Bardo is ultimately not whether the dead can learn to accept their condition but whether the living can acknowledge loss without allowing it to become the organizing principle of existence. Mazzoli’s music gives this recognition an unusually affecting form. Its recurring figures—such as the cello motif that follows Lincoln throughout the cemetery—establish a domain in which consciousness cannot move forward; its moments of lyrical expansion suggest the possibility of release. The drama resides in the distance between the two.

For all its extravagance, Lincoln in the Bardo is most convincing when it abandons the obligation to astonish. The ghosts may require their outlandish costumes, their monstrous bodies, their spectacular departures. Lincoln requires almost nothing: a voice, a child, the terrible persistence of time. This is perhaps the opera’s most difficult truth, and its most beautiful one: that acceptance is not the discovery of meaning in suffering but the recognition that suffering has occurred and that the world, impossibly, continues.

entries.content:
“Mine was a dreary Victorian story,” Anita Brookner told an interviewer in the 1980s. “I nursed my parents till they died. I write out of a sense of powerlessness and injustice, because I felt invisible and passive.” This story was repeated in other interviews in which she performed the part of Anita Brookner, nineteenth-century spinster, art martyr, and monumental melancholic. “I could get into the Guinness Book of Records as the world’s loneliest, most miserable woman,” she told John Haffenden in the Literary Review, one month before winning the Booker Prize, aged fifty-six, for her fourth novel, Hotel du Lac (1984).

Edith Hope, the heroine of Hotel du Lac, writes romances under the nom de plume Vanessa Wilde—the same initials as Virginia Woolf, whom Edith’s friends say she physically resembles. In Wilde’s stories, the powerless and invisible women, or “tortoises,” beat the powerful and competitive “hares,” but this is not how things work in reality, as Edith reminds her agent: there “it is the hare who wins. Every time.” “The facts of life,” Edith concludes, “are too terrible to go into my kind of fiction.” Brookner’s kind of fiction is built on these terrible facts. From the first line of her first novel, A Start in Life (1981), she stayed true to her theme: “Dr Weiss, at forty, knew that her life had been ruined by literature.”

Brookner’s novels are in conversation with other novels, and the title of A Start in Life (published in the US as The Debut) is lifted from Balzac’s Un début dans la vie. Ruth Weiss, the first of Brookner’s overeducated naifs, sees everything and understands nothing. Raised on the belief that “Cinderella shall go to the ball,” she thought adulthood would be “the stuff of literature,” but there are no fairy godmothers for people like Ruth, and the ugly sisters always get the prince. Even her appearance, “exactly half-way between the nineteenth and twentieth centuries,” she “blamed…on literature.” Women’s appearances were of great interest to Brookner, and her own was of great interest to her readers. I can think of no other writer whose cosmetics, clothes, and weight have played such a significant part in the reading of her own character and the reception of her novels. The costume that Brookner adopted as a student—long dark cardigans, neat white frilly blouses, pleated calf-length skirts, sensible shoes, face powder, red lipstick, and an immaculate helmet of amber hair—she retained all her life, along with her slight figure.

Brookner knew to a disarming extent how she appeared to other people: like her avatar in Look at Me (1983), she posed as a woman with “no overt desires or needs…who could be relied upon never to cause embarrassment, either of a social or a personal kind.” There is a witty scene in A Start in Life in which Ruth’s parents, Helen and George, are on a train journey:

Helen was being very charming to a thin woman sitting in the corner of the carriage, although the thin woman was nervous and clearly wanted to read her book.

“Anything interesting?” asked Helen, who intended to talk.

“Henry James,” replied the thin woman repressively.

James was important to Brookner, and Hermione Lee, in her sympathetic and often ingenious new biography, Anita Brookner: Art and Life, identifies the thin reader as one of her subject’s self-portraits.

A Start in Life was written during the summer vacation of 1980, when Brookner was “unhappy,” as she explained in an interview, to the point of being “endangered.” (“For God’s sake,” as one of Ruth’s friends complains, “why do you have to let everything show?”) The following year she gave herself another start in life by changing her Who’s Who entry from “Reader at the Courtauld Institute, born in 1928,” to “‘Professor’ Anita Brookner…born in 1938.” When the deceit was discovered after her Booker Prize triumph she was ridiculed by the press, but elevating her academic status and knocking ten years from her age would seem to be less a sign of vanity than an indication that she no longer, as she told Haffenden, saw herself as “a real person.”

“Alas,” Brookner told her editor in 1981, “I am writing another novel. This one is a real bitch.” Providence (1982) is set at a provincial university where Kitty Maule, who is famous for her sartorial elegance, teaches French Romanticism. In her class on Benjamin Constant’s Adolphe, she explains that “the potency” of the story “comes from the juxtaposition of extremely dry language and extremely heated, almost uncontrollable sentiments…. Even if the despair is total, the control remains.” Brookner’s technique was the same.

Her third novel, Look at Me, was written in the summer of 1982. Frances Hinton, known by her so-called friends as “Little Orphan Fanny,” works as a picture librarian in a medical research institute “dedicated to the study of problems of human behavior.” While cataloging images of madness, she takes notes on “the human comedy” in preparation for her satirical novel. Alone in her former childhood home, Frances feels “a revulsion against the long isolation that writing imposes, the claustration, the sense of exclusion.” But she continues nonetheless because, “swamped in my solitude and hidden by it, physically obscured by it, rendered invisible, in fact, writing is my way…of reminding people that I am here.” Writing Look at Me, Brookner said, made her ill. But her fiction, like that of the Goncourt brothers, whom she admired, was built on nervous illness.

These first three novels, which form a triptych, established Brookner’s motifs: adult orphans, childlike parents, thin heroines, fake friends, dastardly lovers, failed journeys, stifling interiors, disgusting food, loyal housekeepers, the promise—and loss—of Paris, imprisoned existences, and art’s inability to console. “One keeps on writing the same book over and over again,” Brookner regretted, and the reviewers agreed. “More of the Same,” they complained when her annual novel landed in the bookstores. “One thing you can absolutely depend upon,” as the critic Alfred Hickling put it in The Guardian, “is that every July a new Anita Brookner novel will come out and put a dampener on the summer…like rain clouds over Wimbledon.” But the experience of being stuck was her subject. Lee suggests that Brookner’s novels are the same in the sense that Monet’s paintings of Rouen Cathedral or Cézanne’s of Mont Sainte-Victoire are the same. She compulsively returned to her interior landscapes to see them again, in a different light.

Her magnum opus as an art historian, Jacques-Louis David (1980), took fifteen years to complete, but her twenty-four novels—twenty-five if we include her novella, At the Hairdresser’s (2011), published only as an ebook—were each written in three months. She worked swiftly, planning her sentences while walking, and writing in her office at the top of the Courtauld when the building had closed for the summer and winter vacations. She produced only one draft, which needed minimal revisions. None of her books is longer than 275 pages. “Slender means can create a massive effect,” as Brookner said of Braque.

Everything Brookner says about composition, her own or that of other writers, is startling—most of all her comparison of writing fiction to “being on the end of a bad telephone line.” She used the same image to describe Diderot’s “ideal artist,” who must have a “sympathetic nervous system besieged, like an overworked telephone exchange, by an unending stream of sensations and impressions.” Brookner, who knew her Freud, was surely recalling his advice in “Recommendations to Physicians Practicing Psycho-analysis” that the analyst “adjust himself to the patient as a telephone receiver is adjusted to the transmitting microphone.”

She did not undergo psychoanalysis—“It would take too long,” she told Haffenden—but her fiction, she said, was “encoded in the unconscious.” Writing was a process of remembering, repeating, and working through, or rather “trying very hard to remember something which has not yet taken place.” The reason she wrote her first novel at the age of fifty-two rather than thirty, Lee suggests, is that the material needed time to “surface.”

From the start, her approach to fiction was apologetic: she called her novels “small,” “accidents,” an “addiction,” “quite nice but unimportant.” If they gave her readers little pleasure, they gave her even less. Brookner characterized the “perverse energy” of the first four books as

conversion hysteria…. If I could say it I would: as I can’t say it, I have to write it. And I can’t say it because there is no one to listen: people don’t want to hear it. I wish I could cry, scream, stamp, make myself felt, but I can’t.

Given her success in the fields of both fiction and art history, Haffenden said, readers might wonder what it was she wanted to cry out against. “I only ever wanted children,” Brookner replied. “Six sons.” This regret, repeated in other interviews, cannot be taken seriously. The mothers in her fiction are either dead or destructive, while family life is a form of slow suffocation.

Brookner’s “look at me” interviews read like parodies of confessional novels such as Adolphe and The Sorrows of Young Werther, in which, explains Paul Sturgis, the protagonist of her final novel, Strangers (2009), “whole lives were vouchsafed to the reader, with all their shame, yet as if there were no shame in the telling.” Lee, who interviewed Brookner in 1985, suggests that her oversharing was a form of self-defense: the best way to stay hidden is to show you have nothing to hide. It was a complicated ruse because Brookner’s novels satirize the self-display of women who talk only about themselves; one such character in Brief Lives (1990) is the type who “would have revealed all to a biographer, had one been forthcoming.” Invisibility, on the other hand, was a virtue. Brookner praised the novelist Elizabeth Taylor for remaining “invisible behind the screen of her impeccable style,” and she admired how the art historian Kenneth Clark, “an exceedingly complex character…kept his complexities hidden by astonishing and repeated acts of iron control.”

Advertisement

Lee’s aim in Anita Brookner is twofold: to show how the fiction and the art history are of a piece, and to separate the wily, evasive novelist from her gloomy inventions. But first she must find the novelist, and Brookner has not made her job easy. She would “stamp” on “any attempt at biography,” she warned in a 1995 interview: “I have no private papers. I shall leave no trace. That’s the ideal.” Brookner’s novel of 1995 was Incidents in the Rue Laugier, in which Maffy, failing to reconstruct her mother’s life from the cryptic traces left in her notebook, concludes that “the dead, perhaps even more than the living, have a right to their mysteries.” Great swaths of Brookner’s life remain “a mystery,” writes Lee, but the mysteries Brookner planted are part of her story. In many ways, they are her story.

Traces, however, remain, and Lee catches her subject unawares in the unlikeliest of places. Aside from reconstructing Brookner’s life from her notebooks, appointment diaries, address books, dedications, and acknowledgments pages, Lee unearths job references written for her students (“Philip’s character is outstandingly straightforward”), comments on postgraduate essays (“I am sorry that discussions in class do not always match your intelligence”), and exam questions she proposed (“You’re a doctor, and your patient is suffering from terminal Romanticism. What are the symptoms?”). These glimpses make for a more intimate portrait than we would get from the usual sources and add to the rich flavor of the biography.

Lives have witnesses, and Brookner, as Hilary Mantel put it, “was something to witness.” Mantel once watched her at a Spectator summer party where, having arrived, she walked to the end of the garden, nodding and smiling, then walked back again and exited through the front door. “I thought Anita, so oblique and narrow, was acting on the human particles around her without any traceable path, or without ever being located at a single point,” Mantel said. Everyone who met Brookner has a tale to tell, but most of these people, as Lee reminds us, have also read her novels. Seated next to her at a formal dinner, the Irish historian Roy Foster said how much he admired her work. “I don’t like people to talk about my fiction,” she snapped back. “It has brought me more unhappiness than you can know.” Other dining companions recall how in restaurants she routinely ordered the sole, ate half of it, smoked two cigarettes, and left after exactly one hour.

The Anita Brookner uncovered by Lee through interviews with her friends, colleagues, neighbors, and students is a quasi-fictional figure who brings to mind other fictional figures. The story of the vacation during which she felt “endangered” is taken from Villette, in which Lucy Snowe also becomes critically depressed when the Pensionnat de Demoiselles shuts down for the summer. As a cult figure at the Courtauld, Dr. Brookner in her prime was a version of Miss Jean Brodie. Like Muriel Spark’s celebrated schoolteacher, Brookner had her own catchphrase—“It should not be forgotten that…”—and handed out idiosyncratic advice, such as telling an undergraduate with emotional problems to “go abroad and live precariously.” Brookner’s teaching was similarly inventive. Her lectures, prepared “down to the last comma,” were performed, one of her students recalled,

with the utmost coolness and precision, the driest of deliveries, but with a ferocious undercurrent of tension—terror, it seemed, under the most iron control—that transformed them into something passionate and highly dramatic. We listened, hardly breathing, with something of the concentration with which one watches a tightrope walker crossing the high wire.

Brookner’s lecture on The Death of Marat can be read in her monograph Jacques-Louis David (1980):

The scene now shifts to Caen, where citizeness Marie-Anne-Charlotte Corday, after reading her Plutarch, made up her mind to assassinate the friend of the people…. To while away the time, she summoned the hairdresser, then changed into a spotted muslin dress with a pink fichu. A tall black hat with a green cockade and black tassels completed her outfit…. Into her bodice she put her birth certificate, an address to the French people, and the knife. At seven in the evening she took another cab to Marat’s house.

Her lectures on the art criticism of Diderot, Stendhal, Baudelaire, Zola, the Goncourt brothers, and Huysmans were repeated at Cambridge (where Brookner was appointed the first female Slade Professor of Fine Art for the academic year of 1967–1968) and then published as The Genius of the Future (1971). She saw “no connection at all” between Dr. Anita Brookner, reader of paintings, and the fiction writer who turned her gaze on herself: “It’s a sort of schizophrenic activity as far as I’m concerned.”

Lee finds the novelist of emotional intensity at work in the art history and the art historian of “lethally precise observation” at work in the novels. But the differences between Brookner’s two identities are as striking as the similarities. For the first half of her career, she looked into the life of things, and for the second half she wrote about blindness. The epigraph for A Closed Eye (1991), taken from the Henry James novella Madame de Mauves, might be appended to any of Brookner’s novels: “She strikes me as a person who is begging off from full knowledge,—who has struck a truce with painful truth, and is trying awhile the experiment of living with closed eyes.” Frances Hinton, gathering information for her own novel, considers herself “an observer, an unblinking eye.” But the unblinking eye is also an unseeing eye: this was Brookner’s terrifying insight.

Brookner was a Londoner who inhabited the city like an “alien.” “I’ve never been at home here,” she repeated, as though speaking on behalf of her relations. She describes her parents, both from Jewish Polish immigrant families, as “transplanted and fragile people,” “strangers in England” whom she needed to protect. “As a result I became an adult too soon and paradoxically never grew up.” Her mother, Maude Schishka, was a failed singer who suffered from rheumatic fever and a weak heart. By the time Anita—an only child—was fourteen, Maude was a permanent invalid. Her father, a tobacco importer whose understanding of Englishness came from Charles Dickens, changed his name from Nathan Newson Brukner to Newson Brookner. It was “like calling yourself Batehoven,” Anita quipped, but the likeness of his new name to Chadwick Newsome in Henry James’s The Ambassadors must, later, have struck her.

Maude and Newson, according to their daughter, were an ill-suited, tempestuous, and unadventurous couple who lived “outside the natural order…not quite understanding what was happening and being done to them.” Mocked by their “greedy, gossiping” relations, they were excluded from family parties, which made them, in their daughter’s eyes, doubly exiled. Maude, to whom Brookner was not close, thought her the wrong kind of girl to attract a husband, and Brookner later presented her unmarried status as a tragedy. The real tragedy, however, was her parents’ misalliance: their “wretched example,” writes Lee, “gave her a horror of married life.” Her novels equate solitude with loneliness, but staying single, like writing books, ensured self-sufficiency. “Writers,” Brookner believed, “do not and should not move around in groups.”

Her novels are autobiographical but not, as Henry James would put it, in any vulgar, literal way. Brookner turned the peculiar atmosphere of her childhood into Jamesian dramas of innocence and experience. The innocent are the exiles from Eastern Europe, leading half-lives in London mansion flats, and the experienced are monsters of egocentricity who drink life to the lees: overeating, overdressing, preying on the innocent, and laughing in couples. The worst of these figures are the sexually successful women, who don’t read books or ask questions or look inward.

Raised in Herne Hill, southeast London, Brookner won a scholarship to the local girls’ school, James Allen’s. Invited in 1984 to record her memories for the alumni magazine, she replied that “I did not enjoy my schooldays, and for reasons of my own would prefer to keep silent on the matter.” To escape the claustrophobia of home, she visited art galleries; paintings offered “alternative fictions” whose “intelligence and…audacity” raised her spirits. She might have gone to Oxford or Cambridge, but because her parents did not want to lose her, Brookner stayed at home and studied history and French at King’s College London. Her undergraduate years, writes Lee, are among the “many passages in her life which she took care to obliterate,” saying only that she had been “bored.” It was her postgraduate years that changed everything.

By the time Anthony Blunt enters the story, it is clear how much he and Brookner have in common. Both appeared lean, chilly, dapper, and precise, with secretive and compartmentalized lives. “In personal conversation,” she said of her former tutor and colleague, director of the Courtauld between 1947 and 1974, “a blind came down…but in public you got the intimate man.” It was Blunt, described by their mutual friend Francis Haskell as a man who “would take people over,” who gave Brookner her start in life, handpicking her as a master’s student in 1949. It was then that she began to cultivate her appearance and change her diction, making herself as unreadable and unknowable as her mentor.

Having worked for military intelligence during the war, Blunt ran the Courtauld as his personal fiefdom. He refined Brookner’s sensibility, encouraged her love of French neoclassical art, chose as her Ph.D. subject the eighteenth-century genre painter Jean-Baptiste Greuze, supervised her thesis, and arranged a scholarship for her to study in Paris in 1950. Because of him, Brookner therefore managed to escape her parents, and as a punishment they cut off her allowance, leaving her, she said, “literally starving.” Nevertheless, her two years traveling across France “by bus, in fog,” in pursuit of paintings by Greuze, were “the happiest time of my life.”

She defended her thesis in 1952, and in 1956 she was summoned home to nurse her mother. This, Brookner suggests, was the catastrophe of her life, but there were benefits attached, such as slowing the clock and allowing her to retreat from the world. In her novels she used the term “reluctant adult,” and Zoë Cunningham in The Bay of Angels (2001) recognizes, as she nurses her own dying mother, that “above all I should have liked to remain a child.” Brookner’s thirty-nine years at the Courtauld—twenty-five of them under the control of Blunt—provided a similar protection from adulthood. “I’ve never really left school,” she said in an interview for Books and Bookmen in 1983. “That’s my sad story.”

“What happened to the young Anita Brookner,” asks Lee, “set free in Paris, city of possibilities?… Just as she intended, there is an almost complete lack of evidence of her private life.” The suggestion is that she had an affair, but with whom? Some of the witnesses interviewed by Lee thought Brookner’s lover was John White, a poet and former RAF Spitfire instructor. For others “the great love affair” was with Michael Jaffé, a Cambridge professor of fine arts. When one of the students in Kitty Maule’s class on Adolphe asks, “Are they lovers, or what?,” Kitty replies, “We are not meant to know that.” Brookner admired artistic reticence; what took place behind closed doors, she argued, was “all the more powerful for not being shared.” In this sense, destroying all evidence of her private life was an aesthetic statement.

The years between 1956 and 1964 are the “most hidden, the least witnessed and the hardest to describe.” We know that Brookner stayed at home until 1961, when she moved at the age of thirty-three to a flat share near the King’s Road in Chelsea, where we can assume she remained immune to the Swinging Sixties. While giving us glimpses of her subject where she can during these years, Lee turns her attention to Brookner’s criticism—because it was now, in The Burlington Magazine, that she grew her voice. As an art critic she was aloof, opinionated, and very entertaining; in her first review she lamented “the increasing stylelessness of writings on art history,” and her successive articles—on subjects ranging from Paleolithic cave pictures to Pop Art—set out to change this. She found Miró “dull, dull, dull”; Fragonard “turned out a considerable volume of rubbish”; spectators of a large Lynn Chadwick canvas “should crawl up to it, half-mad with dehydration, to get the full impact of that enigmatic non-answer.” David Hockney and Howard Hodgkin, the “jazzy, dizzy Royal College boys,” used paint “in a very narcissistic way”; Van Gogh’s “screaming yellow” portrait of Mme Rondin “shows almost clinical signs of hysteria,” while Kandinsky inspired in her “what the psychoanalysts call a negative response or possibly even a resistance.”

In 1964 Brookner was appointed as the Courtauld’s lecturer in eighteenth-century French art. The post was created for her, very late in the day, by Blunt, in the same year that he was uncovered by MI5 as a former Soviet spy. Granted immunity and protection from public exposure in exchange for his confession and cooperation, Blunt managed to keep his past a secret from his colleagues until the story broke in November 1979. Brookner, who heard the news on the radio, was “astonished.” She nevertheless stood by him during the media storm, paying him visits and bringing him books from the library. “I owe my entire career to Anthony Blunt,” she wrote in a letter to The Spectator in September 1980, the year David was published. When he died of a heart attack three years later, Brookner was one of the few mourners at his funeral.

Lee does not suggest that Blunt, the invisible man, invented Brookner, the invisible woman, or that Brookner became a double agent herself (both novelist and art historian) only after Blunt was uncovered. Nor does she suggest that Brookner’s subject as a novelist—the tragedy of the single life—was a response to Blunt’s own double life. What Lee says about the timing of Blunt’s exposure and the start of Brookner’s second career is that the “story of disappointment, loss of trust and sense of betrayal” was “the kind of plot you might find in a novel by Anita Brookner.”

The impact of Blunt’s deception makes sense of Brookner’s more cryptic comments in her 1984 interview with Haffenden. Five years earlier, she told Haffenden, she had been a different person—“quite buoyant and much more energetic.” Something then happened that changed her view of human character: “If you don’t practice to deceive, as you shouldn’t, it is particularly hard when deception is practiced on you, and you write novels out of that sense of injustice…or you go under.” If her novels were about “anything positive,” she said, “they’re about not playing tricks.” But Brookner’s protagonists are less deceived than they are self-deceiving. Reflecting on the Blunt affair in 1994, Brookner described herself as “too innocent, that’s my fault. I’ve never known”—which is also how she described her parents.

The announcement that Hotel du Lac—“a vindication of the rights of tortoises,” as Brookner put it—had won the Booker was greeted, according to a press report, with “blank and universal amazement.” The favorite on the shortlist had been J.G. Ballard’s Empire of the Sun, and Ballard, a typical hare, accused Brookner of stealing his award. Brookner, of course, agreed that it would have been better had Ballard won. The male critics would not forgive her for overstepping the mark as a middle-aged woman, and the female critics complained that she stayed too firmly within the confines of her narrow remit. Germaine Greer derided Hotel du Lac as “limpid” and “exquisite,” belonging to the “tradition of very sensitive books about lonely ladies in European pensions.” Jeanette Winterson called it “insipid…typical of the way the establishment…rewarded women who are compliant.” According to Joyce Carol Oates, it was “the slightest, least ambitious novel ever to have been awarded a major literary prize.” Brookner’s critical mauling, recounted by Lee with barely concealed rage, makes for painful reading today.

The late novels were received by critics with a change in tone. Instead of more of the same, they saw integrity and unwavering authorial control. Strangers, her final novel, returns to the insight with which A Start in Life had begun: “Life,” Paul Sturgis laments, “was not like a novel.” Reality might be “badly plotted,” as Brookner told Haffenden, but her strange and magnificent body of work was as skillfully crafted as pearls on a string.

entries.title: The Power of Magical Thinking
entries.summary: Carlos Castaneda—sociologist, cult leader, inveterate hoaxer—remains a shadowy figure in Ru Marshall’s new biography.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
American Trickster is the rare book about a cult leader that makes you feel as if you’ve been indoctrinated into a cult. At first the curious reader may experience bemusement, bewilderment, skepticism. What is all this business about chacmools, luminous eggs, the four winds? And whose skeleton was found by hikers near an abandoned mine in Death Valley? Gradually, however, the strange grows familiar. Immersed in a foreign culture, you acquire the language. You become conversant in the practice of Tensegrity and the intellectual development of the sociological subdiscipline of ethnomethodology. Fear not—for those who persist, enlightenment awaits. Bushwhacking through its 658 pages, picking through its thickets of footnotes and endnotes, its digressive swamps, the pilgrim reaches realms of madness and euphoria before settling on a great truth: If our age has a god, or at least a devil, his name is Carlos Castaneda.

Readers younger than sixty may not be familiar with his name, but readers older than six will recognize his cultural legacy. George Lucas modeled Obi-Wan Kenobi after don Juan, Castaneda’s major literary creation. Federico Fellini and Oliver Stone tried in vain to make movies about him; Joni Mitchell named one of her albums Don Juan’s Reckless Daughter; John Lennon, in his final interview, called Yoko Ono his don Juan. “She taught me everything I fucking know,” Lennon said. “I’m married to fucking don Juan.”

Castaneda’s language of psychic self-empowerment has become the native dialect of the self-help industrial complex: his biographer Ru Marshall traces to him the idea of harnessing one’s personal “power,” as well as the belief that one’s “racing mind” can be “stilled” by reflection and exercise. Our political vernacular owes its own considerable debts to Castaneda. The premises that “no reality is superior to another,” that no authority is “purely objective,” that no person’s experience is “more inherently true, real, or valuable” than any other—premises exploited by both the left and the right in recent years—can also be found in his teachings. Once you recognize his catechisms, you see him everywhere.

Until Marshall came along, however, Castaneda was nowhere. Despite his having been one of the best-selling authors on the planet and the leading popularizer (and mythologizer) of Native American spirituality, his legacy was trending toward those of John Gunther, Lloyd C. Douglas, and James Michener. Even Marshall struggles to pin down the essence of Castaneda’s life’s work. Should we think of him as a novelist (masquerading as a sociologist)? A cult leader (masquerading as an intellectual)? Or merely, as Marshall’s title suggests, an inveterate hoaxer in the great American tradition, an heir to P.T. Barnum, Percival Lowell,1 and Charles Ponzi?

“You must create a fog around yourself,” wrote Castaneda, in a passage Marshall uses as an epigraph. “You must erase everything around you until nothing can be taken for granted, until nothing is any longer for sure, or real.” Castaneda’s genius for befogging himself secured his professional success. It also made life tough on his biographers. It is not surprising to learn that American Trickster is the product of twenty years of research, interrupted by crises of self-doubt and epistemic anxieties—twenty years of obsession.

Far more conventional biographers than Marshall would have struggled to resist the impulse to mythologize Castaneda. Even the most unvarnished facts of his life glitter with fabulistic detail, beginning with his birth as César Carlos Salvador Arana on Christmas Day in 1925. Salvador—“savior”—was likely a last-minute addition, reflecting his birth date. Arana translates as a trick, a lie, a hoax. Thus he was born, Marshall points out, with the name “savior trickster.”

Although he told interviewers that he was from São Paulo, Brazil, Castaneda in fact grew up in Cajamarca, an isolated city in Peru’s high northern Andes unacquainted with modern developments in public health. Tuberculosis was endemic, waves of smallpox and bubonic plague passed through, and residents sought medical advice from curanderos—traditional folk healers. Illness was blamed on bad air, witches who took the form of bats and dogs, and duende, imp-like tricksters who lurked at dusk. Common cures included drinking water in which female genitalia had been washed; compresses of chicken feathers matted with bat shit; amulets; herbs; songs. The young trickster developed an early appreciation for the power of magical thinking.

From the time he could speak Castaneda displayed all the qualities of greatness: he was solitary but charismatic, gentle of manner, and a pathological liar. While still a child, he told his friends that he had three children living in the United States. Later he would claim that he had three different mothers. He was Jewish. He was a border spy in Texas. He was a secret military operative who had been castrated in a moonlit knife fight on the mountainous border between Chile and Peru. He was a spy who had lost a testicle to a bayonet in the Korean War. He was his own father.

Advertisement

In our plane of reality, however, Castaneda was born to an upper-middle-class family who owned a house with a courtyard. His mother, Juana Susana Castañeda Novoa, was descended from the least wealthy branch of an aristocratic landowning family. (Upon moving to the United States in his mid-twenties, César Arana would take the name of his maternal grandmother, dropping the eñe.) The man who was likely (but not definitely) Castaneda’s father, César Nemesio Arana Burungaray, was a watchmaker descended from a family of silversmiths and jewelers. Though bookish and withdrawn, Nemesio found his passion as a devoted member of the Alianza Popular Revolucionaria Americana (APRA), a leftist political party that doubled as a religious movement. Its leader, Víctor Raúl Haya de la Torre, practiced astral projection and mesmerism and was directed by voices who spoke to him during trance states. After an Aprista uprising in Cajamarca when Castaneda was nine years old, the Peruvian military massacred thirty of its members. Nemesio and the other surviving Apristas went into hiding. Castaneda came of age in a climate of secrecy, concealment, and strategic dishonesty, under the threat of imprisonment or death.

Cajamarca is transected by underground rivers and streams, including one that surfaced in the Aranas’ courtyard. Some of those rivers, Marshall reports, are fantastical, though “it’s not always clear which is which.”

The most humiliatingly gullible dupes Castaneda ever encountered were also those most responsible for his success: the members of the anthropology department at the University of California, Los Angeles.

Castaneda moved to California not long after his mother died. She was fifty and became ill on a visit to Lima, where Castaneda attended his final year of high school. In the weeks after his mother’s death, Castaneda seduced a thirteen-year-old Chinese Peruvian girl. When she refused to sleep with him, he presented her with a forged marriage license; Marshall calls it the “Trickster’s first written fiction.” She signed the fake document and soon after became pregnant. Upon hearing this news Castaneda booked passage on a cargo ship to San Francisco. From there he made his way down the coast to the city that rewards talented liars with fame, prestige, and fortune.

“Hollywood,” Castaneda told a friend at the time,

has a level of consciousness different from the rest of the world. It produces dreams that do become reality…. People see themselves in the movies, and they begin to act as in a film.

After working apprentice jobs for several years—driving a taxi, cutting hair, making ceramic figurines—he began preparation for his starring role. At twenty-nine (but listing his age as twenty-three), he enrolled at Los Angeles City College. Four years later, despite mostly taking English and creative writing classes, he graduated with an associate’s degree in psychology. In 1959 he enrolled as an undergraduate at UCLA. He was a poor student, earning his best grades in courses that allowed him to cheat. Three of the four A’s he received came in Spanish classes.

He abandoned a second degree in psychology after reading a best-selling book by Andrija Puharich, a physician who received funding from the CIA to study hallucinogenic drugs, astral projection, and ESP. The Sacred Mushroom: Key to the Door of Eternity (1959) is the supposedly true account of a Dutch sculptor who, upon being handed a cartouche that had belonged to an ancient Egyptian queen, plunges into a trance, channels Prince Rahotep, and reveals secret rituals involving magic mushrooms. Puharich shares these revelations with a Mexican curandero, and various telepathic high jinks ensue.2 Castaneda would rip off this premise in every book he wrote.

He switched his major to anthropology. In one class, a professor promised an A to any student who could successfully “interview an Indian.” Out of sixty students, only three did. Castaneda claimed a member of an indigenous community had confided to him details about the ceremonial use of datura, commonly known as devil’s weed. His paper for the class has since vanished, and there is no evidence that he traveled anywhere for it or interviewed anybody. Marshall believes that it secured Castaneda’s admission to graduate school.

He repurposed his paper’s premise for The Teachings of Don Juan: A Yaqui Way of Knowledge (1968), which originated as his master’s thesis. As before, a sober-minded academic becomes convinced, through a series of increasingly implausible encounters, that ingestion of medicinal plants can unlock supernatural powers. Castaneda, searching for another “white-haired old Indian” to interview about devil’s weed, sacred mushrooms, and peyote, encounters a Yaqui elder named Juan at a Greyhound bus station near the Mexican border. Gradually he earns Juan’s trust, then his mentorship.

Advertisement

In his quest for higher knowledge, Castaneda submits to a series of eccentric rituals and demands. He spends an entire night, for instance, trying to find his own personal “spot of happiness” on the planks of Juan’s front porch. He digs deep holes in the desert with his bare hands. For hours, denied drinking water, he grinds datura seeds and live weevils with a pestle. Juan encourages him with gnomic exhortations: “The devil’s weed is only one of a million paths. Anything is one of a million paths…. You must always keep in mind that a path is only a path…. All paths are the same: they lead nowhere.” It’s not quite as good as “Wax on, wax off” (The Karate Kid is another inheritor of the don Juan narrative), but it does the same work. Finally, after bitter bouts of frustration and self-doubt, miracles occur. Castaneda beams back to his childhood home and has a tearful, cathartic reunion with his father. Through a hole in Juan’s hand he sees a vision of himself as an old man. He grows a beak and wings and flies away.

Even putting aside the whole turning-into-a-crow bit, many of the basic factual details of Castaneda’s account buckle under the gentlest scrutiny. The dates given for the visits with Juan contradict his academic schedule. Episodes are shamelessly plagiarized from other anthropological studies of Latin America, including at least one that he was assigned in a graduate seminar. Psychoactive mushrooms are eaten, not smoked. There was no record of the Yaqui using datura in initiation ceremonies. There wasn’t direct bus service from Los Angeles to Nogales. And so on.

How did such obvious fakery get past the august dons of the UCLA anthropology department, let alone the peer review process of the University of California Press? The usual reasons: flattery, laziness, cowardice. A UCLA professor who specialized in Yaqui culture asked for field notes but never followed up when Castaneda ignored his request. Another skeptic gave him the benefit of the doubt. A third, reviewing the book in a prominent journal, assumed that everything was true except the fact that Juan was a Yaqui, and in any case he had no desire to ignite a scandal.

It helped that Castaneda had the enthusiastic endorsement of a powerful colleague, the sociologist Harold Garfinkel, who had developed a new, comically arcane form of philosophy called ethnomethodology, which can be understood, if it can be understood at all, as the critical study of conventional wisdom. Among its central principles is that meaning derives entirely from social cues—an insight that Castaneda exploited ruthlessly to publish The Teachings of Don Juan. Ethnomethodology holds that reality is subjective and constantly under construction, that any appearance of an orderly world is an illusion, and that each of us can alter the course of history if only we change the stories we tell ourselves.

Garfinkel sought to demonstrate his theories with a series of stunts called “breaching” experiments. These were behavioral tests designed to expose the flimsiness of the social order and how easily it could be trampled. In one experiment, a student knocked on a stranger’s door demanding to knock on another door inside the house. In another, a student asked other students, repeatedly, what they meant by various commonplace statements. (“I had a flat tire.” “What do you mean, you had a flat tire?”) A student visited her parents’ house pretending to be a stranger and refused to break character. Today we’d call this “gaslighting.” Or “elder abuse.”

Garfinkel fashioned himself an intellectual descendant of Edmund Husserl, the founder of phenomenology, but Marshall links his practice to a gloomier lineage. Early in his career Garfinkel studied ritual degradation ceremonies; he devoted one paper to determining which public humiliation strategies were most effective at breaking their victims. He understood that disrupting (or breaching) one’s adherence to social convention is the first step toward shaking one’s grasp of reality. It is, in other words, the first step toward brainwashing. He applied these techniques to his relationships with students. Garfinkel, observed one colleague, “behaved more like a cult leader than a scholar.”

It was Garfinkel who persuaded the head of UCLA’s anthropology department to champion The Teachings of Don Juan for publication by the University of California Press and who blocked the resident Yaqui expert from assessing the manuscript. Garfinkel also helped persuade the press not to hold Castaneda to conventional editorial standards. If reality was provisional, who were the gatekeepers of UC Press to insist that their world of fact-checking and verification was superior to don Juan’s visionary “states of nonordinary reality”? To question Castaneda was to question a central ethos of contemporary anthropology: an observer should not impose a “western viewpoint” on a foreign culture but honor that culture’s norms and worldview. If you didn’t take Castaneda at his word, in other words, you weren’t a true anthropologist.

In the Teachings, don Juan ventriloquizes Garfinkel. After Castaneda turns into a crow, for instance, he asks Juan whether it really happened:

“What do you think yourself?”

“Well, I don’t know. All I can tell you is what I felt.”

“That is all there is in reality—what you felt.”

Did Castaneda, who dropped out of UCLA after the publication of The Teachings of Don Juan, care about anthropology? Or writing? Marshall suggests not. Anthropology was simply the most efficient means to an end. The end was a harem.

While Castaneda published eleven additional books, their premise and subject matter remained consistent, as the subtitles indicate: Further Conversations with Don Juan, The Lessons of Don Juan, Further Lessons of Don Juan… His attempts to dress his narrative in factual clothing grew increasingly indifferent, even as critics eventually began to call attention to his more excessive flights of fantasy. At the end of Tales of Power (1974), Castaneda jumps off a mountaintop into an abyss. In The Second Ring of Power (1977), don Juan turns into a ball of light and rises to the heavens. The Eagle’s Gift (1981) reveals that don Juan is a devil. The Fire from Within (1984) introduces the death defiers, vampiric sorcerers who have lived for centuries…

Castaneda applied far more rigor to the project of procuring sexual partners for himself. Marshall traces his cult-building operation to 1960, when he began to pursue two women using psychological tactics he had learned from Garfinkel. By 1970 Castaneda had already developed the mythology of the “four winds”: the quartet of lovers that every “warrior” needed before making his “final journey.” The details of his mythos might appear bizarre, but his recruitment techniques relied on the strategies typically used by cult leaders and other practitioners of psychological manipulation. Marshall quotes the psychotherapist Daniel Shaw: “For those not familiar with cult phenomena, it can be quite astonishing to learn how similar the relationship dynamics are…from group to group.”

Thus Castaneda, like Jim Jones and David Berg and L. Ron Hubbard (whom he admired and tried unsuccessfully to meet), sought out well-educated, affluent women who felt adrift, lacking in purpose. He favored those who had recently experienced an emotional wound, particularly the loss of a father. To “hook” them, to use Castaneda’s term, he showered them with attention and affection. Today we would call it “love bombing,” an expression originally popularized by Sun Myung Moon’s Unification Church. “You’re the last one,” Castaneda would tell his mark. “We were waiting for you. We’re ready to go, but we never expected you to be so smart, so gifted, so beautiful.”

Once Castaneda hooked a woman, he jerked the line. He abruptly vanished from her life, committing her to a hell of uncertainty and self-criticism. Later, upon their reunion, he explained that to return to the group—and leave behind our fallen world for a higher reality—she must prove her loyalty. How? By revealing her deepest secrets (the sine qua non of cult initiation). By committing an act that violated her moral code. By cutting off ties to those “holding her back.” With each additional act she traveled further from rational thought and deeper into Castaneda’s clutches. “Now she must choose between her worldview and the cult’s,” Marshall writes. “This will produce enormous cognitive dissonance. Because she’s completely dependent, she’ll probably choose the cult’s.”

Following the example of Garfinkel’s breaching experiments, Castaneda gave his acolytes lessons in how to avoid hugging their parents; one woman, at his direction, slapped her own mother in the face. He demanded that his disciples collect all their childhood photographs and burn them. He ordered his lovers to cut off most of their hair (the source of their “vanity”), frequently change their legal names, and sever their relationships with their children. They moved to isolated, phoneless apartments. Castaneda lectured one acolyte, in the midst of her debasement, that she would not be able to slip through “the crack between the worlds” if she retained so much as “a scrap of humanity.” Finally he moved them into his inner sanctum: a multifamily house in Westwood Village, where each wind was granted a bedroom. He kept his own bedroom spare: a queen-size bed, a desk, a stand of antique canes he claimed had belonged to don Juan, and a two-pronged dildo that served as a rack for his eyeglasses.

Inevitably Castaneda’s mythology yielded a series of paid “classes,” “practice groups,” and “workshops.” Besides serving as a lucrative source of revenue, the classes helped him recruit new winds, maintain control over those whose commitment seemed to be wavering (usually through public humiliation rituals), and provide make-work for female disciples who had fallen out of sexual favor. Tensegrity, the name he gave this pedagogical enterprise, was, Marshall writes, “both endlessly complex and impossible.” The classes tended to combine self-help pabulum with mystical mumbo jumbo and physical exertions that bore some resemblance to tai chi or Kundalini yoga or torture. A typical instruction:

Bring both hands up all the way above the head and unscrew a hatch at the top of the luminous egg by turning first to the left and then to the right, then back to the left, and then again to the right, and then back to the left, and again to the right.

The acolyte’s confusion was attributed to weakness or disloyalty. The only remedy was deeper commitment.

Reluctantly Castaneda admitted men into his organization when they could be useful: to plant shrubs around his property, to perform repetitive physical movements in Tensegrity classes, and, on Castaneda’s command, to sleep with the less desirable women. The novelist Bruce Wagner, one of his disciples, was enlisted to write a favorable profile of him for Details magazine in 1994. As new cultural trends emerged, Castaneda integrated them into his dogma, speaking of “organic” and “inorganic” beings, for instance, or, with particular irony, “feminist spirituality.”

The constants for Castaneda were power and what it got him. When he was not wooing a new wind or retiring another, he watched old kung fu movies and sipped cappuccinos. The only thing he read—and he read it obsessively, with collegial admiration—was the National Enquirer.

American Trickster often has the bewildering quality of Castaneda’s books, in which the reader breaks into another plane of reality in about the time it takes to gulp down a dram of devil’s weed. Literary biographies, when trained closely on the life and thinking of their subject, tend to feel austere, claustrophobic, solitary; American Trickster is a crowd. To the biographical narratives of Castaneda and almost a dozen of his teachers, acolytes, debunkers, and family members, Marshall adds an intellectual history of ethnomethodology, a history of American hoaxes, a history of religious cults, a history of the trickster mythos, and an earnest, and thereby ludicrous, investigation of the hypothesis that Castaneda actually sold his soul to the devil. One excursus concerns the details of Marshall’s tortured relationship with the University of California Press, the book’s original publisher, a relationship that soured after the press demanded 50,000 words be cut from the manuscript. (Marshall refused and notes ruefully that the press sent American Trickster out for peer review three times—two more times than it had The Teachings of Don Juan.) Another episode finds Marshall coordinating an illegal expedition with the Dezert Rats, a volunteer group that searches decommissioned mines, to look for the remains of Castaneda’s lovers in Death Valley. And a screwball subplot worthy of a Robert Plunket novel follows “the stalkers,” a disillusioned acolyte and her boyfriend who launch an amateurish investigation of Castaneda; they peep on him through gaps in the hedges, observe his workshops from a balcony of an abandoned building across the street, and pick through his trash. (“Sorcerers,” they discover, “don’t recycle.”)

Threaded through Marshall’s narrative are plaintive epistemological riffs on the practice of biographical writing (“What should a biography be?”), which devolve into existential riddles. “What’s a life?” “What’s a fact?” “Who, after all, are we?” It is as if Marshall, who discovered Castaneda in the seventh grade, sought to fill a void of meaning created by the discovery of their hero’s fraudulence. But this quest, too, has its dead ends. In a long footnote concerning Marshall’s laborious if fruitless effort to determine which cars were purchased by one of Castaneda’s wives, they write, “An important question arises: Who gives a fuck? No one.”

That’s not entirely fair, of course. A lot of us do give a fuck. American Trickster poses one of the defining questions of our moment: How do we find meaning in a society so brazenly, proudly fraudulent? Today we bob about in a great plastic garbage patch of breaching experiments. Chatbots love-bomb you while compiling your innermost secrets. Social media connects you with people just like you, who share your interests, approve your politics, and solicit your opinion; should you try to leave, the site comes trailing after you in a series of alerts and pings and discount offerings. Even Google searches, as Marshall points out, deliver results customized to your location and search history. “We believe stories that fit the narratives to which we already subscribe,” they write. “Beliefs—and knowledge—are social.”

So are politics, which draw partisans into Manichaean realms of despair and salvation as divorced from reality as don Juan’s nonordinary realities of sorcerers and death defiers. Marshall traces the lineage of cultlike brainwashing techniques in our national politics back to Donald Trump’s first term and Kellyanne Conway’s championing of “alternative facts.” But the lineage extends back at least as far as the assertion, by an unidentified official, that came to serve as the credo of George W. Bush’s administration: “We’re an empire now, and when we act, we create our own reality. And while you’re studying that reality—judiciously, as you will—we’ll act again, creating other new realities.” Harold Garfinkel, and his prize student, would have nodded with recognition.

Powerful institutions, of course, have always tried to brainwash the masses into loyalty or submission. What’s new is the power of the tools they have at their disposal. Not that it takes much to hook someone, as Castaneda knew well. “Since most people are bored fucks,” he once observed to a group of acolytes in a rare moment of candor, “they’re dying to be told what to do.”

At the end of American Trickster, despite the various missions to Cajamarca and Death Valley and Westwood Village, Castaneda remains a shadowy form—lying in the dark of his Westwood multilevel, sipping his cappuccinos and watching Jackie Chan. Did he ever fall for his own con and believe his own lies? Did he feel remorse for the lives he ruined? Did his sexual and financial successes bring him fulfillment? That Marshall is unable to answer these questions is one of American Trickster’s greatest gifts. It encourages the reader to look elsewhere, and perhaps to look more closely. As a wise man once said:

You have to know when someone is attacking you. Don’t just let it pass. Strike back if that’s what’s appropriate. Avoid them if that’s what’s appropriate. You must be more present in your life.
