El Grillo recounted that once the training period concluded, after being moved around to various ranches and safe houses, the men were taken to a nearby mountain where they faced their final trial, a ritualized ordeal that was called a “graduation.” It took the form of, among other things, a deadly game of paintball, in which the men who fell or performed poorly were butchered by the cartel guards. El Grillo, who was inducted into the cartel, told Romandía that his group consisted at first of around 110 abducted men but that, after the final trial, that number had been reduced to thirty-six recruits, who were only then “accepted” into the cartel and put to work, either as muscle or running drug operations. The rest had been murdered over the course of the so-called training process, especially at the “graduation.” Later, during the final butchery of another “cohort,” El Grillo served as a guard, but did not say how many men he himself was forced to kill.

According to María, some of the men the cartel executed were engineers or doctors who had been abducted to carry out specialized jobs, but the vast majority of the dead were men who had been disappeared in order to undergo a selection and training process for cartel soldiers. “Each day,” she said,

there were two or three people who they [the guards] referred to as “meat for the lions.” When they said: “we’re going to throw this to the lions,” the “lions” were those ovens that you discovered.

As an institution, the so-called training camp is at once a concentration camp for disappeared persons, a place for the selection and training of troops, and a killing field where every “trainee” is expendable. (In the case of Izaguirre Ranch the violence may have extended even further: several of the testimonies in Romandía’s book include allegations of still other gruesome crimes, among them organ harvesting and child abuse, that remain in need of more investigation.) The cartel guards, María recalled, made this last fact perfectly explicit:

As they say: “I’m here today, tomorrow there will be someone else. And if you all are no longer here, there’ll be more trash [más basura] coming in and they will replace you.” There’s a replacement for everyone.

Izaguirre Ranch is not a unique case. It is, Romandía shows, not even a novelty. The model of the cartel “training camp” was pioneered by Los Zetas in the mid-2000s, during a time of intense intercartel warfare. The existence of such camps was known in Mexico mostly through dark rumors until 2019, when the journalists Alejandra Guillén and Diego Petersen published an article about atrocities at two training camps in Tala, just a few miles away from Teuchitlán.1 A less detailed account by a runaway recruit was also published in 2019 about another CJNG camp, this time in Talpa de Allende, also in Jalisco and not far from Tapalpa, the town where the CJNG boss Nemesio Oseguera—known as El Mencho—died in a shootout earlier this year. In 2023, thanks to leaked army documents, the national newspaper El Universal exposed the reach of these institutions: the armed forces had, it reported, destroyed seventy-seven training camps between 2017 and 2023. The article also provided a map with the locations of twenty-seven camps, concentrated in the states of Chihuahua, Zacatecas, Jalisco, and Michoacán.

In Los Zetas’ early days, in the 2000s, most recruits may well have been volunteers.2 But kidnapped “trainees” were present even then, and it is likely that their proportion increased sharply in the years of intercartel warfare and expansion that followed, when the demand for new conscripts outpaced the rate of voluntary recruitment. Conflicts among cartels have the same effect today: in Sinaloa, for example, disappearances more than doubled between 2023 and 2025 amid a war among cartel factions. The number of people who have been disappeared there is close enough to the number of people killed in fighting among the cartels to support the hypothesis that disappearance is, to a significant degree, a strategy of recruitment during times of war.3

The horrors then unfolding at Izaguirre Ranch were ignored by five consecutive municipal governments. Romandía describes the rhythms of everyday life in the municipality of Teuchitlán outside the training camp, including its weekend tourism and patron’s day festivities, civic holidays and Christmas pageants, sporting events and political campaigns, all of which went on undisturbed during the camp’s thirteen years in operation. The municipality of Teuchitlán has comparatively low crime rates, according to official statistics. It is also a place that fosters a kind of circumspection summed up by one local shop worker: “I don’t know whether there are people here who know [cartel members], or whether they’ve attacked anyone from town, but almost everyone avoids them [les sacan la vuelta]. You don’t need to know them to know who they are.”

Advertisement

Even as the justice system did nothing to protect the cartel’s hapless conscripts, the CJNG was quick to make use of it for their own purposes. María told Romandía that the cartel, which frequently “changed houses for security reasons,” periodically outsourced the transit work to the local government: “Sometimes we were even moved by the municipal [police], they transported us like detainees.” El Grillo elaborated on the nature of the cartel’s connections with the state police:

The state police as such was not “bought,” but it was easy to buy. They’d call us themselves. They’d ring the commander and say: “I’m holding a guy who I think is trying to desert [the cartel]. We caught him in the airport. How much will you give me for him?” “I’ll give you five thousand pesos.” “Fine, where shall I hand him over to you? Where do you want me to take him? And where are you going to deposit the money?” “Look, my men will meet you in such-and-such a place. I’ll send you the money and you’ll hand me that cheap little whore [esa puta baratita].” And they’d do the handoff.

In some cases, Romandía reports, the cartel recorded videos of abducted recruits being forced to kill people or dismember bodies, and then used the footage to entrap them. “They made us fight…destroy one another,” one of her sources recalls. “And they taped all of that and then sent the videos to the state attorney general’s office: if we managed to escape, that was the evidence. We were the evidence.” In this way the cartel managed to use Mexico’s distorted criminal justice system as a kind of insurance policy.

The discoveries of the buscadores were a scandal. Dozens of news articles on Teuchitlán were published in the Mexico City press alone. Immediately, and perhaps inevitably, the mountain of shoes and the cremation pits conjured images of Auschwitz. Many articles simply referred to Izaguirre Ranch as a Mexican Auschwitz, or as an “extermination camp.” Photographs, particularly of piles of shoes, circulated globally; stories appeared across the mainstream European and American press.

The government’s reaction was to go on a sustained campaign against the Auschwitz comparison, less by differentiating the Nazi extermination camp from the cartel’s endeavors than by suggesting that crucial information on Teuchitlán had either been planted or deliberately misinterpreted. In a statement on his office’s first findings, the attorney general at the time, Alejandro Gertz Manero, laid the groundwork, building on reports made by his colleagues at the Jalisco state level. “There are human remains” at the ranch, he acknowledged, but the state authorities had yet to provide evidence linking the pits onsite “to the possibility of cremation activities.” The official line, which Secretary of Security and Citizen Protection Omar García Harfuch presented at President Claudia Sheinbaum’s daily press conference on March 24, 2025, was that Izaguirre Ranch was a training camp (not an “extermination camp”) where both volunteers and disappeared persons were brought together to carry out a one-month recruitment program. The government alleged that trainees were compelled to discard their clothes and shoes upon their arrival and were provided with boots and uniforms, implying that the piles of shoes and backpacks did not belong to individuals who had been cremated.

Perhaps a few people had been shot at Izaguirre Ranch, the government admitted. It claimed, however, that there were no crematoria on the site. In a follow-up press conference in April 2025, Gertz Manero alleged that researchers at the National Autonomous University of Mexico had found no signs that soil and rock temperatures at the site had risen past 200 degrees Celsius, far from the eight hundred required to cremate a body. (The Guerreros Buscadores de Jalisco responded with a statement of their own insisting that forensic evidence collected at the state level pointed clearly to cremation.) “They talk about God-knows-how-many things in connection to that place on the basis of a photograph and a few testimonies,” Sheinbaum said. Meanwhile the administration touted a set of concrete measures that it had, it insisted, taken to hold the culprits accountable: the capture of a CJNG boss known as El Lastra, who was the last person in charge of Izaguirre Ranch; the rounding up of around forty suspects; and the passage of yet another package of laws and policies aimed at improving the government’s abysmal track record at finding disappeared persons.

Lower down the official ladder, the assault on the “Auschwitz narrative” was more confrontational. The senate majority leader suggested that the shoes found at the site might have been planted and that the entire affair was a fabrication by the right, implying that the collectives of families of disappeared persons were being politically manipulated. House Majority Leader Ricardo Monreal denounced the opposition as “vultures” for ostensibly exploiting the case. Romandía summarizes the government’s position succinctly:

They claimed there was no evidence of murders, and that the remains could not be confirmed as being human without further analysis. That the notebooks might be old, that the [Santa Muerte] altar proved nothing. That the ranch was not an extermination camp. The word “extermination” was feared most of all.

Although the government made no serious effort to explain the differences between Auschwitz and Teuchitlán, it would, of course, have been correct to do so. There is no comparing them in scale or function. Teuchitlán held perhaps two hundred “trainees” at any given time. If as many as half were regularly murdered over its thirteen years of operation—which the government denies, but some of Romandía’s interviewees claim—the absolute maximum possible number of dead would be in the thousands, in contrast to the documented 1.1 million people who were slaughtered at Auschwitz over a five-year period. The Nazis were not recruiting their soldiers from Auschwitz’s inmates, and the cartel is not in the business of genocide. That the two places relied on similarly atrocious techniques of human degradation did at least finally bring the institution of the cartel “training camp” into the public eye—and yet the comparison also prompted the government not only to whitewash what went on within the camp but also to overlook its position in a broader geography of violence.

The government’s claims were contested both by every eyewitness of the collective’s original discovery and by journalists with decades of experience in the field. In an interview with the investigative reporter Marcela Turati, for instance, the journalist and academic Alejandra Guillén warned against sensationalizing Izaguirre Ranch but nevertheless put the case in the setting of Mexico’s broader disappearance crisis and backed the findings of the buscadores:

There are incinerated remains [at Teuchitlán]. Period. I remember that in Veracruz they referred to such incineration sites as “sites where bodies are destroyed”; in Coahuila, they are known as “clandestine centers for inhumation”; others in recent years prefer to call such places “spots of discovery” [puntos de hallazgo]. What these discussions reveal is that we still don’t have words to name them.4

Guillén acknowledged that “there’s a discussion within the state prosecutor’s office about whether the remains were incinerated there or somewhere else.” But Ruiz, the photojournalist who accompanied the buscadores in March and returned to the site with the media later that month, maintained in a separate interview with Turati that there had been underground crematoria on the premises. None of these authorities question that there was extermination at Izaguirre Ranch. In some sense the distinction between a “training” and “extermination” camp is immaterial here, because in these places killing is integral to the training. Indeed, both terms are equally misnomers, because each is a component part of a single central purpose, which is the transformation of an abducted person into a reliable soldier.

The CJNG’s preference for cremation over other techniques of disposing corpses is known to anyone with experience in Mexican forensics. State commissions for disappeared persons have found untold numbers of cremation sites, and they have sometimes—correctly and appropriately—referred to those places as sites of extermination. In 2021, for example, Karla Quintana, then head of the National Search Commission, declared that there were nine large “extermination sites” in Zeta-controlled areas in Coahuila, San Luis Potosí, Tamaulipas, and Nuevo León where crematoria had been found. A journalist asked Quintana why she used the expression “extermination sites” to refer to such places, objecting that the term “extermination” evoked images of Auschwitz and Birkenau, to which she responded:

We have decided to call them “extermination sites” because of what happened there, because these are illegal crematoria and, in this sense, they are similar to other horrifying episodes in the history of humanity. They are crematoria where the objective is to disappear and pulverize, at least, hundreds of people in order to eliminate all trace of them.

Quintana then named some of the places where such crematoria had been found, including a site at La Bartolina, Tamaulipas, where half a ton of calcinated bone fragments was recovered. She went on to ask why no one in power—no governors or mayors, no federal officials or military personnel—had said anything about what was going on. “The authorities knew,” she said. “It is impossible for something of this scale to happen without authorities knowing what is going on.”

She was, of course, right. But that interview was published five years ago, just a few years after Sheinbaum’s predecessor and mentor Andrés Manuel López Obrador took office. Because the Zetas and the Gulf Cartel had committed those atrocities before the start of López Obrador’s term, Quintana’s exceptionally clear statement was allowed to stand uncontested. There was no reaction by the president, his cabinet, or his party leaders in congress against her characterization of a number of places that are comparable in function and effect to Teuchitlán. At no point back then was the term “extermination site” called into question.

Applying these same terms to the same practices but about a place that was in full operation throughout López Obrador’s presidency is apparently an altogether different proposition. If Teuchitlán, too, was an “extermination site,” that would imply one of two things: either state officials under López Obrador had systematically participated in the atrocities, or a nonstate group had managed to establish and run such a camp outside the state’s jurisdiction, which would imply that the government no longer held the monopoly over the use of force within its territory. The Mexican government can clearly accept neither option.

To forestall any comparison between Teuchitlán and Auschwitz, the government not only obfuscated the meaning of the Izaguirre Ranch findings but may have compromised the evidence itself. Soon after the revelations about the ranch emerged, the government seized control of the site it had previously neglected, and on March 20, 2025, it reopened the area for public viewing. Romandía, who was among the reporters present that day, joined the buscadores and a number of other journalists in accusing the authorities of clearing the property in advance:

What we saw was not a site that was in the process of being investigated, but rather a place that had been meddled with in order to deactivate any reading of a systematic crime…. Everything had been cleaned up: the personal objects that had been found—shoes, underwear, backpacks—had been taken without any indication of where they were or the establishment of a clear chain of custody…. The remains that could still be seen—toothbrushes, spoons, half-buried socks—seemed to have been forgotten or deliberately left on the ground. Some mothers knelt and started to dig with their hands. One father dug a blue Adidas backpack out of the ground, suggesting the carelessness of the authorities that had allegedly already safeguarded all the evidence in the state attorney general’s office and packed it for forensic evaluation.

Contaminating crime scenes, neglecting chains of custody, stonewalling, sequestering and distorting information, capitalizing on media distractions: this sort of deliberate forensic bungling—what I am tempted to call “governed incompetence”—is a leitmotif of Mexico’s justice system. It has thrived under political leaders of every stripe, from Vicente Fox to Claudia Sheinbaum, in response to atrocities as varied as the femicides in Ciudad Juárez during the 1990s, the 2010 massacre of seventy-two migrants in San Fernando, the 2011 and 2012 massacres in San Fernando and Cadereyta, the forty-three missing Ayotzinapa students in 2014, and the clandestine burials in municipal mass graves found in Tetelcingo and Jojutla, Morelos, in 2015 and 2016. López Obrador and Sheinbaum have not tired of protesting that they are “not the same” as their predecessors, but in this regard all governments do seem to have been created equal.

In 2022, for instance, under López Obrador, Romandía sent a freedom of information request to Mexico’s Secretariat of National Defense asking for the number of clandestine training camps it had dismantled. The ministry responded that it raided 415 clandestine camps between 2018 and 2022, but refused to differentiate between training camps—an institution that thrives on enforced disappearance—and every other sort of cartel encampment. Following a similar approach, the press release announcing the National Guard’s 2024 raid on Izaguirre Ranch did not even mention that the place was a training camp. Had the Guerreros Buscadores de Jalisco not intervened, the nature of Izaguirre Ranch would never have been known. A few months after the scandal broke, a set of prominent arrests were made—including the former mayor of Teuchitlán—and 141-year sentences were meted out to the ten men who were captured in the September 2024 raid. But the prosecutors’ findings in their interrogations of these men have not touched higher levels of government, nor did they lead the authorities to admit that there were mass killings at the site.

Because the Izaguirre Ranch case is part of a broader system, investigations could conceivably entangle a variety of government officials both high and low. The extent of the case’s implications became clearer when the CJNG’s leader, El Mencho, was killed this past February, allegedly in a shootout with state security forces. Izaguirre Ranch was a cog in El Mencho’s business empire, and among the scattered documents that journalists found in his cabin were payments to a variety of low- and mid-level government officials, including in municipalities where cartel training camps have been found, such as Talpa, Tala, and Teuchitlán. On March 16, 2026, however, the current attorney general, Ernestina Godoy Ramos, announced that her office had failed to secure the chain of custody over the evidence found in El Mencho’s residence. As a result, those account books and papers now likely have no legal standing.

The previous media scandal of this size—the case of the Ayotzinapa students in 2014—permanently hobbled Enrique Peña Nieto’s presidency. It is hardly surprising, then, that the government has turned its back on the cause of the disappeared, even failing to protect the leaders of the buscadores from persecution. On April 24, 2025, a member of the Jalisco collective named María del Carmen Morales was murdered along with her twenty-six-year-old son.

Mexico’s attorney general’s office marked the first anniversary of the uncovering of Izaguirre Ranch by the buscadores with an official communiqué. Their investigation, it explained, “has clearly and forcefully established that the place was used as a training ground, which can be deduced from the fact that it was used for activities such as target practice, workouts, and physical challenges.” The announcement mentioned no cremation site and stated that the genetic materials of only one person were isolated. Forty-seven individuals were detained in the case, it claimed, without elaborating on who they were or what they revealed about the place.

As for the clothes found on the premises, which helped inspire the international reaction, the press release accounted for them in a single line: “According to our information, in this training camp people were recruited by force and their belongings, such as their clothes, were taken from them so that they might put on another kind of garment [para portar otro tipo de vestimenta].” Which other “kind of garment” was not specified. There is amply aired testimony of phones, IDs, and valuables being stripped from abductees, but none of Romandía’s witnesses mentioned anything that might support the government’s claim that recruits were asked to exchange their clothes. After all, providing captives with uniforms would be an unnecessary expense for the cartel, both because so many of the recruited members must be indistinguishable from regular civilians in order to do their work and because so many of them are murdered as part of the so-called training. Why give every abducted person a uniform upon arrival, when most will falter in the selection process?

El Grillo’s is the only testimony in Romandía’s book that mentions a cartel-sponsored change of clothes, and it occurs immediately after his final “graduation,” an ordeal from which he and the other survivors emerged battered and badly shaken by the killing and incineration of those who failed the tests. Once they traveled to the town near Puerto Vallarta where they would be stationed, the cartel guards told the survivors, “the person in charge of the house will cure your wounds. He’s going to buy you some clothes, they’ll give you a cell phone, and you’ll start earning money.” This is not a change in “kind of garment,” but rather the purchase of a fresh set of clothes for the survivors of a harrowing and murderous selection process.

The official communiqué, finally, did not acknowledge that when the National Guard first secured Izaguirre Ranch, it made no mention of “a training ground.” Now that the attorney general’s office does use that phrase, it still has nothing to say about how, exactly, one “trains” an abducted captive to become a cartel soldier against his will. But the testimonies in Romandía’s book do have something to say about this. “We are rankled by the fact that they [the media] now call [Izaguirre Ranch] ‘la escuelita del narco’ [the narco’s little schoolhouse],” the informant known as María says, “because you don’t go there to learn.”

On October 10 Italy’s TG1 public television channel aired an interview by the journalist Stefania Battistini with a masked man who claimed to have been directly involved in the incineration of around 250 people at Izaguirre Ranch. “We disappeared hundreds of people,” he declared. “I know exactly where their remains are.” The former CJNG hitman also said that he shared intelligence with the Guerreros Buscadores de Jalisco, a claim that was corroborated by the collective’s leader Indira Navarro, who said that they found incinerated remains in several other places thanks to information he provided. ​The office of Mexico’s attorney general denied the man’s account. They have now processed 92 percent of Izaguirre Ranch’s grounds, they report, and have found no further remains.
